newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cattle-on-feed numbers rising, but still low.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cattle-on-feed numbers rising, but still low.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department is expected to report fed cattle supplies on September 1 in major U.S. feedlots were less than a year ago, but the pace at which cattle moved into feedlots has quickened, analysts said.
The average of analysts' estimates for the number of cattle on feed in the seven primary cattle-feeding states was 89.9 percent of a year ago, in a range of 88.2 to 92 percent.
However, August placement estimates averaged 112.7 percent of a year ago in a range of 106.6 to 119.0 percent. On feed supplies started August at 86 percent of last year.
Weather and high feed prices warranted keeping cattle on grass longer than usual, this year in some areas.

"We had great summer grazing conditions that allowed cattle to stay longer and high priced feed was certainly an incentive to leave them outside (of feedlots) as long as you could, to put more weight on them. This all pointed to a bunching of the placement numbers in the mid- to late-part of the summer," said Tippens.
Many analysts are looking for heavy placements through October which could build feedlot numbers fairly quickly.
On feed supplies have risen from 86 percent on August 1 to the estimated 89.9 percent of last year on September 1.

"Cattle feeding returns were very positive in August and that's usually a good indicator that they are going to buy these (cattle)," said Jim Robb, director of the Denver-based Livestock Marketing Information Center.
"With the reduced placements over the last several months there was a lot of empty pen space at feedlots," Robb said.
He noted that many feedlots were reporting that only 50 percent of pen space was in use coming into August.
But grain prices began slipping late in the summer from record-high levels as the fall harvest approached.
Also, feeder cattle supplies were large. The only question was, how long they stayed out on grass, Robb said.
Based on estimates for rising placements and on-feed supplies, there will be more cattle available for market from November through January, Tippens added.

Marketing estimates for August ranged from 92 to 98 percent and averaged 94.7 percent. Analysts noted there was one less marketing day which accounted for most of the decline in the percentage versus a year ago.
